title: Awake after naloxone, now sleepy again

brief.situation: 23:00 in the PICU. You are the nurse for Mia, 2 years old, 13 kg, admitted from the emergency department after she was found at 19:30 with her grandmother's open bottle of liquid methadone. She was apneic and pinpoint on arrival, woke after one dose of the ordered naloxone at 20:10, and has been on continuous pulse oximetry and capnography since.
handover: She was playful until about 22:30. Her mother asks whether she can go home in the morning since 'the antidote worked'.
Her grandmother is not sure how much was missing.

Unit standing order for opioid toxicity: the nurse may give the ordered repeat naloxone dose for a respiratory rate under the ordered threshold or apnea and calls the intensivist at once for any recurrence of respiratory depression; a naloxone infusion is started on the intensivist's order. The poison center has been called.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Rousable only to a firm rub, then drifts off; pinpoint pupils again.
Respiratory rate has fallen from 24 to 13 over an hour with shallow breaths; end-tidal CO2 has climbed from 38 into the high 40s.
Ingestion before 19:30; the single naloxone dose at 20:10; drowsy again from about 22:30, consistent with naloxone wearing off while the long-acting opioid persists.

why.question: Why is Mia sleepy again, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Naloxone is short-acting and methadone toxicity in children can be delayed and prolonged; recurrent drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, a falling respiratory rate and rising end-tidal CO2 mean recurrent opioid toxicity.
parts.modelAnswer: The naloxone has worn off and the methadone hasn't. She's hard to rouse with pinpoint pupils again, her breathing's slowing and her CO2's climbing.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Gives the ordered repeat naloxone, supports the airway with oxygen and a bag-mask ready, keeps the alarms, calls the intensivist at once for an infusion, and explains the need for prolonged observation.
parts.modelAnswer: Give the repeat dose, open her airway with oxygen and the bag ready, keep the alarms on, call the intensivist for an infusion, and tell her mom she's staying a while.

apnea.headline: Apnea
apnea.body: Methadone outlasts naloxone. Recurrent sleepiness, pinpoint pupils and a rising CO2 mean the opioid is winning again: repeat naloxone, support the airway and call.

safe.headline: Recurrence caught
safe.body: You saw the recurrence, gave the repeat dose, supported her airway, kept the alarms and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

safeGaps.headline: Treated, with gaps
safeGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether she was left to sleep, and whether the alarms were widened.

scoring.modelReasoning: Methadone toxicity in children can be delayed and prolonged, and naloxone's half-life is short, so respiratory depression recurs and early discharge carries a high risk of death. Mia has recurrent drowsiness, pinpoint pupils, a falling rate and a rising end-tidal CO2: give the ordered repeat naloxone, support the airway with oxygen and a bag-mask ready, keep the alarms, and call the intensivist at once for a naloxone infusion with continuous capnography and pulse oximetry and a long observation period.

choices.label: Only after a long observation off naloxone; early discharge carries a high risk of death
In the morning if she looks well

obsQ.explain: Children with methadone exposure have a high risk of death with early discharge; extended observation after the last dose is needed.
